This underscores the need to emphasize reading education in the elementary years when the foundation of literacy is established. This study aims to improve the reading, comprehension, and motivation of 4th-grade students through ChatGPT-4, which generates texts based on their own prompts. The study was conducted ARTICLE IN PRESS in two public primary schools located in the center of Bursa, Türkiye. The research group consisted of 106 students. The study employed a sequential explanatory mixed method design. The quantitative aspect of the study was conducted using the Solomon four-group experimental design, while the qualitative part was carried out through a case study. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test, Independent Samples t-test, ANOVA, and effect size calculations, while qualitative data were examined using descriptive and content analysis. According to the findings, when the experimental groups were compared with the control groups, statistically significant differences were identified in favor of both experimental groups with respect to reading and comprehension skills as well as reading motivation. These differences showed a high effect size across all dependent variables. Based on these findings, it is recommended that teachers integrate ChatGPT to help students generate appropriate texts during free reading periods. Introduction Thanks to rapid advancements in information technologies, artificial intelligence applications capable of mimicking human behavior are now being utilized across various fields (Jia, 2023). Due Sto these developments, ChatGPT, one of the artificial intelligence applications, is increasingly being used to enhance educational environments (Elmas et S al., 2024). This has led to a growing interest in research focused on determining ChatGPT's contributions to students' E learning processes (Mahapatra, 2024; Woo et al., 2024). One of the areas these studies focus on is the development of students' reading skills and reading motivation. The significance oRf such studies stems from the profound impact of reading on an individual’s personal and academic life. A positive relationship has long been established between the P development of students’ reading skills and their academic success (Anderson et al., 1985). Moreover, this relationship fosters the growth of cognitive skills that are essential for sustained academic achievement (James et al., 2024). N Reading and comprehension are not only essential for students’ academic success but also fundamental competencies they will rely on throughout their lives (Moss et al., 202I4). Moreover, proficiency in reading and comprehension plays a crucial role in achieving social success, and fosteri ng these skills is a fundamental responsibility of education(Lorch E & Broek, 1997). In this regard, reading and comprehension can be enhanced through a variety of pedagogical interventions (Olimova & Gilyazetdinov, 202L4). Enhancing students’ reading skiClls and motivation has been the focus of numerous studies. In these studies, while traditional teaching methods have been preferred (Fatimah et al., 2024; Ibrahim, 2017; Miller & Meece, 1997; I Nevo & Vaknin-Nusbaum, 2020; Notanubun et al., 2024; Permatasari & Wienanda, 2023), technology-supported T approaches have also become more widespread in recent years (Anggrainy et al., 2024; Gea et al., 2024; Hong, & Lee, R 2023; Hossu, & Roman, 2023). Interactive reading applications, audiobooks, multimedia resources, and artificial intelligence play a crucial rAole in enhancing reading skills and motivation (Rofi'i et al., 2023). Alongside research on artificial intelligence, the impact of teaching methods on students’ reading skills should not be overlooked (McLean, 2007). The integration of technology into instruction has proven effective in developing elementary students’ comprehension skills (Chuyan & Dong, 2023). In this regard, the present study distinguishes itself by incorporating AI-supported texts and activities alongside traditional teaching methods. Furthermore, a review of the literature on ChatGPT’s role in developing primary school students’ reading skills shows that existing studies have focused on areas such as general reviews (Jendia & Ismail, 2023)(Jendia & Ismail, 2023), the readability of ChatGPT’s responses to students’ questions (Murgia et al., 2023), its integration into primary school learning (Kockova et al., 2023), and its use in teaching foreign languages (Wotsa & Yadav, 2023). This study differs from previous research by focusing on the enhancement of reading, comprehension, and reading motivation in the mother tongue, addressing decoding difficulties, and exemplifying a triadic interaction model through the integration of artificial intelligence into a teaching approach grounded in teacher–student interaction. ChatGPT enables students to take responsibility for their own learning by making them active in the text creation process. In this context, the practice employs a hybrid model in which students’ prompts shape the creation of texts and activities for mother tongue education, and these texts are subsequently implemented through established teaching methods. Reading and Reading Motivation ARTICLE IN PRESS Reading and comprehension, fundamental to communication and the foundation of knowledge acquisition and professional expertise, are complex and transformative processes that shape thinking and perception (Olimova & Gilyazetdinov, 2024). Reading remains central to daily life and plays a vital role in information acquisition (McCarthy & Yan, 2024). Reading is a fundamental pillar of education, enabling students to engage effectively with learning activities, acquire knowledge, analyze and interpret information, and develop critical thinking skills (Madaminova, 2024). Classroom activities, assignments, and all forms of reading materials—books, stories, articles, and chapters— are ultimately rooted in comprehension (Pearson, 2014). Reading is an essential skill for learning, allowing students to access and benefit from educational materials independently. Therefore, if students fail to develop adequate reading skills in early education, they may face difficulties in later stages of schooling and in their subsequent lives (James et al., 2024). The true measure of success in reading is comprehension (Moss et al., 2024; Paige et al., 2024). According to Kintsch (1979), defining comprehension in all its dimensions is extremely difficult. Kirby (2007) argued that reading comprehension operates in a bottom-up manner, progressing from sentences to details, then to main ideas, and ultimately to overarching themes. With the help of words, more abstract ideas are derived from sentences based on grammatical rules. Understanding at the level of ideas represents a more superficial interpretation of the text. Through interaction, these ideas are synthesized to uncover the main ideas, from which thematic generalizations and abstractions are derived. In reading comprehension, readers construct an abstract model of the situation described, moving beyond the cognitive processing of individual words (Van Dijk & KintSsch, 1983). Successful comprehension is largely dependent on the effective formation of this mental model (Moss et al., 2024). During reading S comprehension, individuals perform cognitive tasks that link words, sentences, and paragraphs to construct a coherent E mental representation of the text. At the same time, they use metacognitive skills to monitor the coherence of these representations and make necessary adjustments (Soto et al., R2019). These skills enable readers to monitor comprehension by being aware of their cognitive processes during reading and regulating subsequent actions to P achieve learning objectives (Schraw & Dennison, 1994). Collins and Smith (1980) proposed a two-process model that conceptualizes comprehension as an active N process. The first component involves monitoring comprehension. In this stage, readers take corrective actions to address potential failures, such as difficulties in undIerstanding relationships between words, sentences, or larger textual units. The second processing skill involves u sing clues in the text to generate, evaluate, and revise hypotheses E about current and future events. At this stage, readers consider variables such as text type, events, and character traits. They make predictions about the progression Lof the text by forming hypotheses, testing their accuracy, and interpreting its key points. Predictions concern what mCay occur, whereas comments focus on interpreting what is already present in the text. These two skills are interdependent and closely connected. For instance, temporary hypotheses can be I formed regarding the meaning of a word or sentence. Generating a hypothesis or making a prediction may concern T the overall text, but it can also focus on the meaning of a word or sentence at the micro level. The main goal of the R reading model is to help students identify potential comprehension challenges during silent reading and develop the skills to overcome them. ToA achieve this, practice sessions are conducted under teacher supervision during read-aloud activities. Over time, the teacher’s guidance gradually diminishes, enabling students to apply the model independently while reading. In the final stage, the goal is for students to apply these skills while reading silently. According to Gough and Tunmer’s (1986) Simple View of Reading, reading comprehension (R) consists of two components—decoding (D) and language comprehension (C)—and is best represented by a multiplicative model (R = D × C). Linguistic comprehension is also referred to as listening comprehension. The multiplicative relationship indicates that comprehension cannot occur without both word recognition and language comprehension. For instance, if R = D × C and C = 0, then R equals 0. Gough and Tunmer illustrate this with the example of a five-year-old child who can use and understand language but cannot read due to underdeveloped word recognition skills. According to this model, comprehension is high only when both word recognition and language comprehension skills are strong. If word recognition is strong but language comprehension is weak, comprehension remains low. Similarly, if language comprehension is strong but word recognition is weak, comprehension also remains low (Georgiou et al., 2009). Apart from the Simple View of Reading, it can be stated that there are three traditional theories that explain the reading process. The first of these is the Bottom-up Theory, which focuses on the decoding (D) component of the Simple View of Reading. According to this theory, reading begins when the units that constitute the text are received by the reader as visual input (Ada Amadi, 2019). From the smallest units—phonemes to syllables, syllables to words, and words to sentences—meaningful fragments are formed and subsequently integrated to construct overall comprehension (Field, 1999). Each operation performed and the hierarchically structured data serve the purpose of reaching meaning. In this respect, it can be argued that the model explains reading by placing the text at the center. Advocates of this model contend that in order for students to acquire higher-level comprehension skills, they must first develop automaticity in the foundational skills of early literacy (Mondesir & Griffin, 2020). ARTICLE IN PRESS Another theory is the Top-down Theory, which focuses on the linguistic comprehension (C) component of the Simple View of Reading. This theory emphasizes an interaction between the reader and the text in which the reader’s prior knowledge, experiences, predictions about the text, hypotheses, and expectations are actively engaged (Zhang, 2010). In this model, the reader reconstructs meaning by drawing on these expectations regarding the text (Pourmohammadi, 2016). Therefore, unlike the Bottom-up Theory, the Top-down Theory can be said to place the reader at the center. The third theory is Interactive Reading, which integrates the processes of the Bottom-up and Top-down theories (Stonavich, 1980). Interactive Reading is a model based on the interaction established between students and an adult before, during, and after reading. During the reading process, participants listen to one another, evaluate ideas, and collaboratively engage in activities to read and comprehend the text. In this process, students’ interests, needs, and background knowledge about the text play an active role (Ashford, 2024). This process ensures that students remain active both affectively and cognitively. Interactive Reading is grounded in the principles of encouraging the child’s active participation in reading, fostering language use, providing feedback on language production, and enabling the adult to adapt their own reading practices to the child’s linguistic abilities (Pillinger & Wood, 2013). When implemented in the early years, it facilitates the resolution of potential reading difficulties (Morgan & Meier, 2008). In this study, this reading approach was adopted. In the common practice of Interactive Reading, listening and speaking skills are employed alongside reading skills. Within the scope of the research, since the interaction began during the text-generation process, the adopted approach allowed for the obSservation, assessment, feedback, and development of all students’ language skills. S Hirsch (2003) proposes three principles to enhance students' reading comprehension: fluency, vocabulary, E and domain knowledge. Fluency enables the reader to focus on comprehension; a broad vocabulary facilitates understanding and learning; and domain knowledge—also referreRd to as prior subject knowledge—supports both fluency and vocabulary, thereby fostering deeper comprehension. These three principles are closely interconnected. P Fluent students who can pronounce words quickly and accurately are able to master decoding and concentrate on comprehension without overloading their memory. If decoding is slow, previously decoded words may be forgotten N during the ongoing process, which can hinder comprehension of the text. Students can overcome the limitations of working memory by reading fluently, recognizing wordIs rapidly, and applying basic grammatical rules. Fluent readers can focus on comprehension because they have auto mated many of the fundamental processes involved in reading. A E broad vocabulary supports fluent reading, as students are already familiar with the words. Domain knowledge, defined as the reader’s familiarity with the text’s cLontent, also contributes to this process. Students with prior subject knowledge tend to read more fluently onC a given topic, as they are familiar with it and have already encountered the relevant vocabulary. Experts in a subject can read texts related to that subject more fluently, as their prior knowledge I enables them to process information more efficiently and draw inferences by connecting new material with what they T have already learned. R The critical role of vocabulary knowledge in determining reading comprehension success has been widely recognized (Sidek & RaAhim 2015). A strong relationship exists between vocabulary richness and reading comprehension (Torgeson et al., 1997). Because word recognition involves repeated cognitive activation during reading, comprehension is considered to depend on successful word decoding (Perfetti, 2007). Verhoeven and van Leeuwe (2008) state that the relationship between vocabulary and comprehension is reciprocal: vocabulary expands through reading, and comprehension improves as vocabulary develops. In proficient readers, decoding and comprehension are closely integrated, and both skills are typically well developed. In contrast, weak readers tend to have difficulties in both decoding and comprehension, with each skill reinforcing the other’s weakness (Shankweiler, 1999). Reading fluency is closely linked to comprehension (Fuchs et al., 2001). Reading fluency is an indicator of advanced reading skills (Reis et al., 2008). Poor fluency leads to slow word recognition. As a result, previously recognized words may be lost from working memory before subsequent words are processed, hindering their integration For readers who struggle with fluency, the first step is accurate reading. However, focusing too much on accurate word pronunciation may hinder overall comprehension. Thus, attention to accuracy at the word level is often associated with inadequate comprehension (Cain, 1999). Since reading supports both individual and societal development, it is essential for students to cultivate a love of reading and sustain their interest in it (Seventilova, 2024). According to Bartlett (1932), understanding a text involves active and constructive cognitive processes rather than passive and receptive ones. During this process, readers continuously build a mental representation of the text by using their prior knowledge. This active process requires a willingness to engage in reading. Reading motivation influences whether students develop positive or negative attitudes toward reading. Students with high reading motivation exert the necessary effort and use strategies ARTICLE IN PRESS to comprehend the text, as they recognize the challenges of the reading process (Ahmadi et al., 2013). The effort and persistence needed for comprehension are fueled by reading motivation (Baker & Wigfield, 1999). As motivation increases, reading and comprehension skills improve accordingly (Larson et al., 2016). When students relate what they read to their own experiences, their motivation to read increases (Briggs, 2010). Texts that are unrelated to students’ interests weaken their reading motivation (Guia et al., 2024). Low reading motivation contributes to difficulties such as limited vocabulary, poor decoding skills, lack of fluency, and weak phonological awareness during reading and comprehension (Kheang et al., 2024). Sharing their thoughts and comparing them with others engages students in the learning process and fosters their reading motivation (Wahidah, 2018). Reading motivation can be cultivated through an enjoyable classroom environment, engaging reading activities, and texts aligned with students' interests (Mohseni Takaloo & Ahmadi, 2017). To foster reading motivation, it is important that students are active in the reading and comprehension process, that texts match their interests, that they can relate what they read to their experiences, and that they are supported in overcoming limited vocabulary. Since ChatGPT offers features that support students in these areas, it has been considered a motivational enhancer in this study. 2.2. ChatGPT and Its Use in the Learning Environment Artificial intelligence applications offer significant opportunities to enhance reaSding and comprehension tasks, which have become increasingly complex in modern life. These technologies support students' reading comprehension by S providing materials appropriate to their level (McCarthy & Yan, 2024). Applications accessible through technological E tools such as tablets and smartphones can help students with reading difficulties improve their skills (Sand et al., 2024). R In addition, multiple Large Language Models (LLMs) were utilized with respect to students’ reading skills. P Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) was employed to address students’ attention difficulties during reading and to analyze reading comprehension questions (Chen & Wu, 2020; Fernandez et al., N 2022); The Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5) was utilized to provide a reading comprehension model, generate questions, and produce answers (Guan et al., 2024; GuIo et al., 2024); The Cross-lingual Language Model–RoBERTa (XLM-R) was applied to perform multilingual infere ntial reading and comprehension tasks across different languages E (Choi et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021) Beyond these models, the Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (ChatGPT), developed by OpenAI, has been widely adopLted in the enhancement of reading skills. ChatGPT is an artificial intelligeCnce–based application designed to generate text in response to user prompts (Halaweh, 2023). ChatGPT is a large language model that improves its outputs through deep learning. It draws on a I vast repository of texts and images from the internet to generate responses to user prompts. With the support of DALL- T E, it allows individuals in interactive learning environments to create visuals tailored to their preferences (Rospigliosi, R 2023). While some perspectives encourage the use of ChatGPT, others emphasize its potential negative impacts (Adeshola & Adepoju, 202A3). Halaweh (2023) describes these concerns as issues that accompany every technological development. Despite differing opinions, ChatGPT has found applications in education. The use of ChatGPT and similar technologies in education has become an unavoidable reality (Loos et al., 2023). ChatGPT, which can generate human-like texts, differs from other language models by focusing on how people express themselves, aiming to establish more natural communication and meet their needs (Yusuf, 2023). Susnjak and McIntosh (2024) examined ChatGPT's ability to perform high-level cognitive tasks and generate human- like text, noting that it can apply critical thinking skills and produce highly realistic output with minimal input. As a continuously developing model, ChatGPT allows updates to be made to the generated texts (Brown et al., 2020). For students to create a mental representation of a text during comprehension, their prior knowledge of the underlying structures must be sufficient (Eleman & Oslund, 2019). Based on this, students whose comprehension skills are below expectations can improve by strengthening their prior knowledge. ChatGPT enables students to supplement missing prior knowledge in the generated texts. Students can address these gaps by asking ChatGPT questions in areas where their prior knowledge is insufficient. Furthermore, responsibility for the comprehensibility of a text lies primarily with the author (Adams, & Bruce, 1982). In texts generated with ChatGPT, students who take responsibility for composing the text also review it for language and narrative features to improve overall quality. According to Gunter and Kenny (2008), discussions among readers can encourage reflection on the events and concepts presented in a text. In this context, ChatGPT–student–teacher interaction enables discussion and reflection on the text by drawing insights from three sources. Thus, discussion and reflection on the text become possible through insights contributed by ChatGPT, students, and teachers. Murgia, Pera, Landoni, and Huibers (2023) evaluated ChatGPT's performance based on responses to online questions from 9–10-year-old fourth-grade students with different literacy levels, in relation to the elementary school ARTICLE IN PRESS curriculum. Analysis of student feedback revealed that ChatGPT's responses were appropriate for the fourth-grade level. Hidayat (2024) recommends that educators and administrators use AI-based applications to improve students' reading skills, based on his findings. Xiao, Xu, Zhang, Wang, and Xia (2023) examined the use of ChatGPT to create reading materials and comprehension activities for facilitating English learning among middle school students. The study found that ChatGPT generated texts more effective than those created by humans. Bezirhan and von Davier (2023) tested the appropriateness and readability of texts generated by ChatGPT-3 for fourth-grade students. Experts reviewed the generated texts and concluded that they were suitable for the students’ level. Additionally, Lin and Chen (2024) showed that, beyond text generation, ChatGPT can produce multiple-choice tests comparable to human-made ones for developing and assessing students’ comprehension skills. Findings from the literature confirming ChatGPT's potential to generate questions for text creation and comprehension assessment serve as the primary motivation for this study. As an advanced AI tool, ChatGPT possesses the ability to generate prompt-based texts, revise generated content in line with new prompts, and even create images that reflect the text. These features made it a suitable choice for the present study, as they directly support the research aims. Study Model I E This study employed a mixed-method approach, defined as a technique that integrates quantitative and qualitative research methods (Johnson & OnwuegbuLzie, 2004), together with Creswell’s sequential-explanatory design (QUAN→qual). In this design, the researCcher first collects and analyzes quantitative data, followed by qualitative data collection to gain deeper insights (Creswell & Clark, 2015). Related quantitative and qualitative data are integrated in I the discussion and interpretation sections. The core principle of this design is that combining quantitative and T qualitative approaches is more effective for problem-solving than using either approach alone (Creswell, 2014). R The quantitative component of the mixed-method design employed the Solomon four-group experimental design. This design is an apAproach that aims to address the pre-test sensitivity issue while retaining the advantages of conducting a pre-test, by randomly assigning participants to either receive or not receive the pre-test and intervention program (Gagnon & Barber, 2018). The design consists of four procedural stages. First, four groups are formed. Second, two groups receive a pre-test. Third, the intervention program is applied to one pre-tested group and one non- pre-tested group. Finally, all four groups take a post-test (Huck & Sandler, 1973). In this context, four 4th-grade classes, as detailed in the next section, were selected. The groups to be tested or not tested, as well as the classes designated to receive the pre-test, were randomly assigned, and the pre-tests were administered. Following the implementation of the experimental design, a post-test was administered to all classes The qualitative component of the study employed a holistic single-case study design. A case study is a research method that provides a detailed understanding of a situation, or in other words, a case bounded by specific spatial and temporal conditions (Gustafsson, 2017). With this approach, real-life problems can be explored in depth (Ratnasari & Sudradjat, 2023). The holistic single-case design complements traditional research by capturing phenomena and details within a single case (Zaytseva & Bao, 2015). In this context, the interaction between the students participating in the experimental application and ChatGPT-4 was treated as a single case. Through interviews with students, this interaction was explored from multiple perspectives. The use of ChatGPT not only enhances students’ reading comprehension by encouraging their active participation in the instructional process (El Hassan & Alsalwah, 2025) but also enriches their vocabulary (Young & Shishido, 2023). In addition, ChatGPT is capable of analyzing user-generated prompt sentences, deciphering their semantic structures, and producing appropriate texts accordingly (Hadi et al.,, 2023). Due to these features, ChatGPT was incorporated into the intervention program within the research model. Error Analysis Inventory The inventory was developed by Akyol (2019), drawing on the works of Harris and Spay (1990), Ekwall and Shanker (1998), and May (1986), to determine students’ reading levels. Using this inventory and its accompanying tables, students’ word recognition and comprehension percentages can be calculated. Three levels were defined to interpret the percentages: the Free Level, referring to the student’s ability to read and understand the text without support; the Instructional Level, referring to the student’s ability to read and comprehend the text adequately with the support of a teacher or adult; and the Frustration Level, referring to the student’s limited understanding of the text and frequent reading errors. These categories make it possible to determine the reading levels of elementary and middle school students." When applying the inventory, it is recommended that the text contain 25–100 words for first- and second- graders; 100–200 words for third- and fourth-graders; 200–300 words for fifth- and sixth-graders; and 300–350 words ARTICLE IN PRESS for seventh- and eighth-graders. It is also suggested that texts be selected from one grade level below the student’s current level and that the student’s reading be recorded using a voice recorder. By identifying reading error types— such as addition, repetition, and finger tracking—and the symbols representing them, the usability of the inventory was improved. The word recognition percentage was determined by matching the total number of words in the text with the number of misread words in the relevant table. For example, if a student read a 192-word text with five errors, the table entry corresponding to 191–195 words with five errors indicates a word recognition rate of 97%. In order for a reader to be considered at the independent reading level, the word recognition percentage must be at least 99%. Readers whose recognition percentage falls below 90% are classified as being at the frustration level. Students’ comprehension levels can be assessed through multiple-choice or open-ended questions. In this study, open-ended questions were preferred, and students’ comprehension was measured using six questions: three requiring literal understanding and three requiring deep understanding. The literal comprehension questions were scored as follows: two points for a complete response, one point for a partial response, and zero points for no response. The deep comprehension questions were scored as follows: three points for a complete and effective response, two points for expressing more than half of the expected response, one point for a partial response, and zero points for no response. A student’s comprehension percentage was calculated by dividing the score obtained by the maximum possible score if all questions were answered correctly. For example, a student assessed with six open-ended questions can obtain a maximum of 15 points—six points from the three literal comprehSension questions and nine points from the three deep comprehension questions. I f this student provides a complete response to one literal comprehension S question (two points), a partial response to another literal comprehension question (one point), and complete responses E to two deep comprehension questions (six points), while leaving the remaining questions unanswered, the student receives a total of nine points. The student’s score (9) is then dividRed by the maximum possible score (15), resulting in a comprehension level of 60%. Discussion and ConcluAsion In the study examining the effects of texts created with students’ prompts using ChatGPT-4 on reading, comprehension, and reading motivation, significant differences were found in favor of the experimental groups for all variables. As a result of the study, the comprehension scores of the experimental groups improved to a statistically significant degree compared with the control groups. In the qualitative research group, six students (E1S7, E1S6, E1S22, E1S25, E2S7, E2S17) reported that their comprehension skills had improved. Similarly, in a study conducted by Gharaibeh and Basulayyim (2025) with primary school students experiencing reading and comprehension difficulties, it was found that the comprehension scores of the experimental group significantly increased compared with those of the control group when supported by ChatGPT. In another study, Al-Otaibi and Al-Homidhi (2025) examined the effects of ChatGPT on second-language comprehension skills and determined that the experimental group demonstrated notable development in both creative and critical comprehension abilities. In a meta-analysis of 51 studies conducted between 2022 and 2025, the effectiveness of ChatGPT in learning environments was examined, and it was determined that ChatGPT had positive effects on students’ learning, perception, and higher-order thinking skills (Wang & Fan, 2025). In the qualitative research group, three students (E1S5, E2S2, E2S16) stated that the texts were creative; three students (E1S6, E1S8, E1S10) indicated that the texts increased their sense of curiosity; one student (E1S5) expressed that the texts helped them recognize their own creativity; and two students (E1S6, E2S7) reported that their imagination improved. When the quantitative and qualitative findings of the study are considered together with the existing literature, it can be concluded that the ChatGPT-supported intervention enhanced students’ comprehension skills in a way that also encompassed variables such as curiosity, imagination, and creativity. Bus, Shang, and Roskos (2024) examined studies conducted between 1970 and 2020 within the scope of independent reading practices outside of traditional classroom reading activities, and reported an overall significant effect size for word recognition, decoding, fluent reading, and reading attitudes. Similarly, Alqahtani (2024), in a meta-analysis of studies involving students with reading difficulties, found that technology-based intervention programs had a substantial effect size. It can be stated that this intervention, which yielded results consistent with the literature, offers a strong model that teachers can employ to support students’ reading skills. In this research group, the texts generated by ChatGPT based on students’ prompts enhanced their reading, comprehension, and reading motivation. This outcome can be integrated with multiple learning objectives included in curricula, such as vocabulary enrichment, making inferences, and identifying the main idea and theme. The widespread availability of internet access in schools, along with the use of computers, projectors, and smart boards, can facilitate the integration of student-generated prompts with curricular objectives. In this way, artificial intelligence can be incorporated both in language classes and during free reading periods, thereby fostering the development of students’ reading and comprehension skills. JSON: Name: chatgpt4_student_prompt_reading Title: A mixed-method Solomon four-group evaluation of ChatGPT-4–generated, student-prompted texts to improve fourth-grade reading accuracy, reading comprehension, and reading motivation Short Hypothesis: Providing fourth-grade students with reading texts and associated activities generated by ChatGPT-4 from the students' own prompts will produce greater gains in reading accuracy, reading comprehension scores, and reading motivation than standard teacher-led reading instruction over a 10-week intervention. Related Work: Prior approaches to improving elementary reading combine teacher-led strategies (bottom-up, top-down, interactive reading) and technology-supported interventions (multimedia, audiobooks, gamified apps). Recent work using large language models and transformer architectures has explored automated question generation, readability assessment, and text/task generation for reading practice; studies report strengths in producing grade-appropriate passages, on-demand vocabulary support, and automated item generation. Existing research limitations include: few randomized or Solomon-design controlled trials at primary-school grade levels; many studies focus on foreign-language learning or model-readability evaluation rather than integrated classroom outcomes; evaluations often compare AI outputs to no-treatment baselines rather than to matched human-authored texts; lack of ablation on prompt provenance (student vs researcher prompts) and teacher mediation; small samples and narrow socio-demographic settings limiting generalizability; documented LLM failure modes (hallucinations, repetitive phrasing, occasional syntactic errors) not systematically quantified in classroom deployments; and sparse reporting on ethical/data-privacy constraints for minors. Abstract: This research operationalizes a classroom-integrated pipeline in which fourth-grade students generate prompts that feed ChatGPT-4 to produce short reading passages, comprehension questions, and visuals; these AI outputs are deployed within teacher-mediated interactive reading sessions. The study addresses whether student-prompted, ChatGPT-4–generated materials produce measurable improvements in reading accuracy, comprehension, and reading motivation compared to standard instruction. Contributions are threefold: (1) a controlled Solomon four-group experimental evaluation with pre/post measurement on validated reading and motivation instruments; (2) an ablation comparing student-prompted AI texts, researcher-prompted AI texts, and human-authored texts matched for readability; and (3) a qualitative case study of student experience and prompt evolution. Expected outcomes include statistically significant, high-effect-size gains in reading accuracy, comprehension, and motivation for the student-prompted AI condition, plus empirical characterization of prompt quality effects and common AI output error modes relevant to classroom use. Experiments: Dataset and participants: four intact fourth-grade classes (N = 100–120, target n≈105), drawn from two public primary schools, randomly assigned to a Solomon four-group design (E1 no pre-test + treatment, C1 pre-test + no treatment, E2 pre-test + treatment, C2 no pre-test + no treatment). Intervention: 10-week program, 4 class-hours/week (80 hours total), with twice-weekly cycles: (a) session A: students create prompts; ChatGPT-4 generates passage (100–220 words), six comprehension items (3 literal, 3 inferential), and one visual; (b) session B: teacher-mediated read-aloud/interactive reading using printed materials. Baselines: (1) standard instruction (control groups), (2) human-authored texts matched to ChatGPT readability and length, (3) ChatGPT-4 texts generated from researcher-crafted prompts (prompt-provenance baseline). Ablations: (A) student-prompted vs researcher-prompted vs human-authored; (B) refined prompts (teacher-assisted prompt-refinement) vs raw student prompts; (C) teacher-mediated vs fully digital delivery; (D) visuals included vs visuals omitted. Instruments and metrics: Error Analysis Inventory (word-recognition and oral-reading error count), comprehension score (open-ended scoring; max 15), Reading Motivation Scale (21-item 4-point Likert), reading fluency (words correct per minute), vocabulary acquisition (pre/post targeted word list), qualitative semi-structured interviews (n=20 purposive). Readability control: calculate Ateşman readability scores to match human-authored baseline texts. Statistical analysis: power analysis prior to enrollment (target effect size d=0.40, α=0.05, 1-β=0.80); normality checks (skewness, kurtosis), Mann–Whitney U for non-normal variables, Independent Samples t-test, ANOVA with Games–Howell post hoc where appropriate, Solomon-design specific comparisons to assess pre-test sensitization, eta-squared for effect size; report 95% CIs and pre-registered primary outcomes (reading error count, comprehension score, motivation score). Qualitative analysis: descriptive and content analysis with participant coding (e.g., E1S1), triangulate with quantitative outcomes. Data collection schedule: pre-tests for designated groups in week 0, 10-week intervention, post-tests for all groups in weeks 11–12. Missing data handling: document attrition and apply intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: ChatGPT-4 hallucinations (incorrect facts), repetitive or stereotyped phrasing across generated stories, occasional inverted or awkward sentence constructions, variable dialogue density and emotional tone. Prompt-dependency: learning gains may vary strongly with prompt clarity and teacher prompt-refinement, producing heterogeneous treatment effects. Measurement and evaluation biases: reliance on open-ended scoring and self-report reading motivation scale can introduce rater bias and social desirability bias; pre-test sensitization effects despite Solomon design may persist. Data and privacy constraints: processing student prompts and outputs through cloud LLM raises legal and ethical constraints for minors and may limit deployment in some jurisdictions. Implementation fidelity: teacher variability in mediating AI materials and classroom management differences may confound outcomes. Access and equity: results may not generalize to schools without reliable internet, device access, or to different SES, linguistic, or cultural contexts. Scalability and compute: real-time generation for large cohorts requires API capacity and may incur cost and latency issues. External validity: study conducted in a single language (Turkish) and grade level (4th) limits cross-linguistic and age generalization. Statistical power risks: if true effect sizes are smaller than anticipated, sample may be underpowered for subgroup and ablation comparisons.
